atoms.text: The designed failure: a product is engineered to break after a set period, so reliability is deliberately withheld.
The annual model: last year's version is made unfashionable by restyling, so desire is scheduled.
The information asymmetry: the maker knows the product's lifespan and the buyer does not, so every purchase is a rigged bet.
The replacement cycle: sales depend on shortening how long things last, so the economy requires waste.
The repair that is impossible: a device is sealed or glued so it cannot be fixed, so ownership excludes maintenance.
The brand loyalty trap: a customer is expected to replace like with like, so dissatisfaction is captured by the same company.
The competitor who lasts: a durable foreign product forces domestic makers to build better, so competition can undo the scheme.
The engineer's integrity: a designer refuses to build in failure and loses market share, so virtue is punished by the system.
The landfill as product afterlife: discarded goods pile up out of sight, so consumption exports its consequences.
The software that stops updating: a working device is made useless by dropped support, so obsolescence moves from hardware to code.
The repair café: a community resists disposal by fixing things together, so maintenance becomes political resistance.
The warranty that expires: protection ends exactly when failures begin, so the contract is timed against the customer.
The object that outlives its owner: a well-made tool is inherited while newer ones fail, so durability is a family legacy.
The subscription upgrade: ownership is replaced by rental, so the company retains control of the thing you use.
The planned scarcity: parts are discontinued to force replacement, so supply chains are weapons.
The secret memo: internal documents reveal the failure schedule, so the story's evidence is a corporate confession.
